surveyDefinition.title: Smartwatches — consumer survey (Germany)
surveyDefinition.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on usage intensity, purchase motivations, and trade-off priorities in the European smartwatch market.

segments.name: Health-Focused Users
segments.description: Wear the watch primarily for continuous health and fitness tracking (heart rate, sleep, workouts). They check the app daily, value sensor accuracy above all, and are willing to pay a premium for advanced health features.

segments.name: Connectivity-Driven Users
segments.description: Use the watch mainly for notifications, calls, and quick glances at messages. They treat it as an extension of their phone, value seamless integration with their smartphone ecosystem, and are less concerned with deep health analytics.

segments.name: Style-Led Buyers
segments.description: Choose a smartwatch as a fashion accessory and personal statement. They care about design, materials, and customization options, and are willing to pay for aesthetics even if functionality is basic.

segments.name: Price-Sensitive Buyers
segments.description: Want the core smartwatch functions (notifications, basic fitness tracking) at the lowest possible price. They compare deals, wait for promotions, and are quick to switch if a cheaper alternative meets their needs.

surveyDefinition.whatThisSurveyIs: A segmentation study of Smartwatches buyers in Germany. It asks how people use Smartwatches, how they choose it, and what would make them switch — then sorts respondents into the behavioural groups defined below. Questions stay at category level: no named brands, and nothing about adjacent categories.
surveyDefinition.whoseContextThisIs: Adults in Germany who buy or use Smartwatches for personal or household use. Respondents qualify if they: Individuals who currently own or have purchased a smartwatch in the past 12 months; Individuals who are actively considering purchasing a smartwatch within the next 6 months; Must be the primary decision-maker for their own smartwatch purchase. Excluded: Businesses or institutions purchasing smartwatches in bulk for employees; Children under 18 (unless the study specifically targets kids' smartwatches, which is not the default); Individuals who only use basic fitness bands without smart features.
surveyDefinition.whyTheseRespondents: Consumers buy smartwatches for personal use, pay for them out of pocket, and decide on the model and brand themselves. While some businesses may purchase smartwatches for employees, the dominant and defining buyer is the individual consumer, making this a pure B2C market.
respondentBehaviours: Health and fitness tracking (steps, heart rate, sleep)
Brand loyalty to smartphone ecosystems (Apple, Samsung, etc.)
whatIsDeliberatelyNotAsked: Age or household income as behavioural questions — no finding in this survey is driven by them. They are asked once, at the end, in Profiling, and used only to cross-tabulate the behavioural results.
Brand, company or manufacturer names — the survey stays at category level so findings are not tied to one competitor set.
Where the respondent lives — region is chosen when viewing the results, so asking it again would waste a question.
surveyDefinition.howToReadTheNumbers: Percentages are modelled estimates built from published market evidence — they are not measurements from fielded interviews, and should be read as an expected shape of response rather than a result. Single-choice, ranking and rating-scale questions sum to 100%. Multi-select questions do not — each option is an independent share of respondents choosing it. The N shown on each question is the display base for that item.

structure.storyline: Questions run in a planned narrative order: broad and easy first, specific and sensitive last.
structure.storylineSummary: The survey opens by establishing who owns a smartwatch and how it fits into their daily life, then moves into the purchase journey — what triggered the buy, where they researched, what they paid, and which features decided it. Next it probes what they truly need from the watch, including battery, design, and compatibility, and forces trade-offs to reveal value priorities. It closes with satisfaction, pain points, switching triggers, and upgrade intent, so the segments can be distinguished by their usage patterns, purchase motivations, and future behaviour.

targetCustomer.summary: Adult consumers of Smartwatches in Germany — who Individuals who currently own or have purchased a smartwatch in the past 12 months; Individuals who are actively considering purchasing a smartwatch within the next 6 months; Must be the primary decision-maker for their own smartwatch purchase. The audience is defined as individual consumers who buy smartwatches for personal use, as they are the primary purchasers and users. The qualifiers ensure we capture both recent buyers and those in the market, while exclusions remove B2B bulk purchases and non-smart wearables to keep the study focused on the consumer smartwatch segment.

questions.question: Which single feature mattered most when you chose your smartwatch?
questions.insight: Top response: Battery life (30.00%).

Work with my phone's operating system

questions.question: How long should a smartwatch battery last between charges?
questions.insight: Top response: 4-6 days (35.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Battery life is a top pain point; most segments demand at least 4-6 days, with a strong minority wanting 7+ days. Only a small fraction accepts daily charging.

questions.question: How acceptable is it to charge your smartwatch every night?
questions.insight: Top response: Not at all acceptable (40.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Price-Sensitive and Health-Focused Users strongly reject nightly charging; only a small minority of Connectivity-Driven Users find it acceptable.

questions.question: Which strap and case materials would you prefer for a smartwatch?
questions.insight: Top response: Silicone strap (55.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Silicone straps are popular among Health-Focused and Price-Sensitive Users; Style-Led Buyers prefer metal and leather. Eco-friendly materials are a niche interest.

questions.question: How important is it that your smartwatch works seamlessly with your phone?
questions.insight: Top response: Very important (40.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Connectivity-Driven Users and most other segments treat phone integration as essential; only a tiny minority downplays it.

questions.question: What would you give up to pay less for a smartwatch?
questions.insight: Top response: Premium materials and design (45.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Price-Sensitive Buyers are most willing to sacrifice premium materials and advanced sleep analysis; Health-Focused Users are less willing to give up accurate sensors.
questions.beatTitle: What they would give up for a lower price

questions.question: What is the most you would pay for a smartwatch that meets all your needs?
questions.distributionNote: Price-Sensitive Buyers concentrate in the under €150 and €150–€249 brackets; Health-Focused and Style-Led Buyers are spread across mid-to-high tiers, with a small premium segment.
questions.beatTitle: How much they would pay for the ideal watch

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied are you with the Smartwatches you currently use?
questions.insight: Top response: Somewhat satisfied (35.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Overall satisfaction is moderate; pain points like battery and price temper higher satisfaction.

questions.question: How likely are you to recommend the Smartwatches you currently use to a friend or colleague?
questions.insight: Top response: 8 (20.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Health-Focused Users and Connectivity-Driven Users show moderate to high likelihood, while Price-Sensitive Buyers pull the mid-range down slightly.

questions.question: Which aspects of your smartwatch satisfy you most?
questions.insight: Top response: Health and fitness tracking (42.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Health-Focused Users dominate satisfaction with tracking; Connectivity-Driven Users value notifications; Style-Led Buyers are a smaller but notable group.

questions.question: How likely are you to buy a new or replacement smartwatch in the next 12 months?
questions.insight: Top response: Somewhat likely (32.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Positive sentiment and a strong growth outlook push intent toward 'likely'; Price-Sensitive Buyers temper the top end.

metadata.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on usage intensity, purchase motivations, and trade-off priorities in the European smartwatch market.
metadata.segmentation_lens: Jobs-to-be-done combined with price sensitivity: the same smartwatch is hired for fitness tracking, notifications, style, or health management, and buyers differ sharply in how much they will pay for those jobs. This lens separates buyers more meaningfully than usage frequency alone, because a daily

segments.name: Health-Focused Users
segments.description: Wear the watch primarily for continuous health and fitness tracking (heart rate, sleep, workouts). They check the app daily, value sensor accuracy above all, and are willing to pay a premium for advanced health features.
segments.hypothesis: They will report high usage frequency, prioritize accuracy and advanced health metrics over style, and show low price sensitivity when accuracy is proven.

segments.name: Connectivity-Driven Users
segments.description: Use the watch mainly for notifications, calls, and quick glances at messages. They treat it as an extension of their phone, value seamless integration with their smartphone ecosystem, and are less concerned with deep health analytics.
segments.hypothesis: They will prioritize notification reliability and ecosystem compatibility, show moderate usage frequency, and be willing to switch brands if compatibility improves.

segments.name: Style-Led Buyers
segments.description: Choose a smartwatch as a fashion accessory and personal statement. They care about design, materials, and customization options, and are willing to pay for aesthetics even if functionality is basic.
segments.hypothesis: They will rank design and brand image above technical specs, show lower engagement with health features, and be less sensitive to price when the watch looks premium.

segments.name: Price-Sensitive Buyers
segments.description: Want the core smartwatch functions (notifications, basic fitness tracking) at the lowest possible price. They compare deals, wait for promotions, and are quick to switch if a cheaper alternative meets their needs.
segments.hypothesis: They will report lower spend, prioritize price over advanced features, and show high switching likelihood when a comparable watch is discounted.

fieldingNotes.recommendedSample: n=800-1,200 for stable segment-level sub-groups (roughly n>=312 per segment after weighting). At n=1,000 the margin of error on a whole-sample percentage is about ±3.1pp at 95% confidence; on a segment of n=200 it widens to about ±6.9pp, so segment-level differences under ~10pp should not be reported as real.
fieldingNotes.quotaControls: Apply quotas on the category-usage and frequency screeners so heavy users — who are more willing survey-takers — are not over-sampled.
scriptingNotes: Rotate the order of answer options on every non-ordinal question to remove primacy bias. Do NOT rotate ordinal scales (frequency bands, price bands, satisfaction) — their order carries meaning.
Anchor 'Other', 'None of these' and 'Prefer not to say' to the bottom of the list, exempt from rotation.
Every 'Other' option takes an open-text capture, coded back into the frame at analysis if any single verbatim exceeds 3%.
No routing or skip logic: every respondent sees every question, so the base is constant across the instrument.
Include one attention check in the middle third — a standard instructed-response item. Terminate on failure and replace.
Randomise the order of the two ranking/trade-off items between respondents so neither is systematically answered while fresher.
caveats: Percentages in this document are modelled from published market evidence, not measured from fielded interviews. Replace them with primary data once the study is run.
Ranking items are shown as a lighter-weight ranking exercise; run them as MaxDiff if you need more precision on driver importance.
Profiling questions are for cross-tabs only and are excluded from the segmentation scoring model.

metadata.storyline_summary: The survey opens by establishing who owns a smartwatch and how it fits into their daily life, then moves into the purchase journey — what triggered the buy, where they researched, what they paid, and which features decided it. Next it probes what they truly need from the watch, including battery, design, and compatibility, and forces trade-offs to reveal value priorities. It closes with satisfaction, pain points, switching triggers, and upgrade intent, so the segments can be distinguished by their usage patterns, purchase motivations, and future behaviour.
storyline_notes: Chose jobs-to-be-done as the primary lens because smartwatch buyers differ more in what they hire the watch for (health, connectivity, style, price) than in how often they wear it.
Added a dedicated beat on battery life in preferences_expectations because it is the top pain point in the market profile and a key differentiator between segments.
Added a beat on phone compatibility and ecosystem fit because non-Apple compatibility is a major issue in Europe, especially for Android users.
Included a trade-off beat to reveal price sensitivity and value priorities, which is essential for separating the value-seeking segment.
In the buying_behavior section, placed price_paid before decision_drivers to avoid anchoring on price before understanding what matters.
In satisfaction_future_intent, added a specific pain-points beat to capture the top frustrations from the market profile, and an upgrade-intent beat to understand future purchase plans.
metadata.classification_reason: Consumers buy smartwatches for personal use, pay for them out of pocket, and decide on the model and brand themselves. While some businesses may purchase smartwatches for employees, the dominant and defining buyer is the individual consumer, making this a pure B2C market.
